title: Output, Plotting and Data Files
intro: Results live in memory as vectors until you print, plot or write them. This page covers choosing what to save, the text and rawfile formats, the plotting commands (plot, gnuplot, pyplot, hardcopy), and how to read ngspice results into Python.

items: By default every node voltage and every voltage-source and inductor current is saved, and nothing else.
save v(out) i(VDD) @m1[id] (or .save in the netlist) saves only what is listed. save all @m1[gm] keeps the defaults and adds a device quantity. Saving less makes big transients faster and smaller.
save nointernals (version 45) drops internal device nodes, which OSDI models such as PSP add in large numbers.
.option savecurrents saves all device terminal currents (@r1[i], @m1[id], @q1[ic] ...). .probe (alli, a device current, a differential voltage, power p(M1)) is a selective form.
set interp, or .option interp, keeps only points on the tstep grid.

blocks.source:
print, wrdata and write
V1 in 0 PULSE(0 1 0 1u 1u 5u 10u)
R1 in out 1k
C1 out 0 1n
.control
  save v(in) v(out) i(V1)
  tran 0.1u 20u
  print v(out)[50] v(out)[100]
  set width=120
  print col v(in) v(out) > out-table.txt
  set wr_singlescale
  set wr_vecnames
  option numdgt=7
  wrdata out-data.txt v(in) v(out)
  write out-binary.raw v(in) v(out)
  set filetype=ascii
  write out-ascii.raw v(in) v(out)
.endc
.end

items: print prints vectors as a table (print col, the default for long vectors) or in a line (print line). > file sends it to a file. set width and height set the page size; set nobreak removes page breaks.

wrdata file vectors writes plain columns of numbers: by default each vector comes with its own scale column (time, v(in), time, v(out)); set wr_singlescale writes one scale column, set wr_vecnames adds a header line, option numdgt sets digits. This is the easiest format for gnuplot, a spreadsheet or numpy.loadtxt.

write file vectors writes a SPICE3 rawfile, binary unless set filetype=ascii. Without vectors it writes the whole current plot; with -r on the command line batch runs write everything automatically. load file.raw reads one back as a plot.
wrs2p writes Touchstone S-parameter files; eprvcd writes digital event nodes as a VCD file for a waveform viewer such as GTKWave; sndprint writes a .wav sound file (version 47).

plot v(in) v(out): an X11 window (Linux, with --with-x) or the Windows GUI window. Options: xlimit 0 1u, ylimit -1 1, xlog, ylog, loglog, title 'text', xlabel, ylabel, vs for a different x axis (plot v(out) vs v(in)), and retraceplot. The window can zoom, and hardcopy saves it as PostScript.
gnuplot name vectors: writes name.plt and name.data and runs gnuplot. With set gnuplot_terminal=png/quit it writes a PNG without opening a window, for batch runs.

pyplot name vectors (version 47): the same with Python and matplotlib; set pyplot_terminal=png writes name.png, set pyplot_subplots=N stacks the traces in panels, set pyplot_style picks a matplotlib style.
asciiplot: a character plot in the terminal, from the SPICE2 days; quick on a remote shell.
iplot: an incremental plot that updates while a transient runs.
Xschem, KiCad and Qucs-S show results in their own viewers; gaw and GTKWave read rawfiles and VCD files.

blocks.text: wrdata files load with numpy.loadtxt. For rawfiles, packages exist (spicelib, PyLTSpice, ltspice), but the format is simple enough to read directly: a text header with Variables: and Values: or Binary: sections, then the numbers, real doubles (or pairs for complex data) point by point. This reader handles ngspice's binary and ascii rawfiles, real and complex, and checks itself against the files written above:

blocks.source:
# read_raw.py: read an ngspice rawfile (binary or ascii, real or complex) into numpy arrays
import numpy as np

def read_raw(path):
    plots, f = [], open(path, "rb")
    while True:
        meta, names = {}, []
        line = f.readline()
        while line and not line.strip():          # blank lines between plots
            line = f.readline()
        if not line:
            return plots
        while line:                               # header lines "Key: value"
            text = line.decode("latin-1").rstrip("\n")
            key, _, val = text.partition(":")
            key = key.strip().lower()
            if key == "variables":
                for _ in range(int(meta["no. variables"])):
                    parts = f.readline().decode("latin-1").split()
                    names.append(parts[1])         # index, name, type
            elif key in ("binary", "values"):
                break
            else:
                meta[key] = val.strip()
            line = f.readline()
        nv, npts = int(meta["no. variables"]), int(meta["no. points"])
        cplx = "complex" in meta.get("flags", "").lower()
        width = 2 if cplx else 1
        if key == "binary":
            data = np.frombuffer(f.read(8 * nv * npts * width), dtype="<f8")
            data = data.reshape(npts, nv * width)
        else:                                     # ascii: "index value" then one value per line
            need, toks = npts * (nv + 1), []
            while len(toks) < need:
                toks += f.readline().decode().split()
            rows = [toks[i * (nv + 1) + 1:(i + 1) * (nv + 1)] for i in range(npts)]
            data = np.array([[float(x) for t in r for x in t.split(",")] for r in rows])
        if cplx:
            data = data[:, 0::2] + 1j * data[:, 1::2]
        plots.append({"title": meta.get("plotname"), "vectors": dict(zip(names, data.T))})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = read_raw("out-ascii.raw")[0]["vectors"]
    b = read_raw("out-binary.raw")[0]["vectors"]
    print(sorted(a), len(a["time"]))
    assert np.allclose(a["v(out)"], b["v(out)"], rtol=1e-6)
    d = np.loadtxt("out-data.txt", skiprows=1)    # wrdata with a header line
    assert np.allclose(d[:, 2], b["v(out)"], rtol=1e-6)
    print("v(out) at the end:", b["v(out)"][-1])

blocks.text: The test at the bottom reads the same results in the three formats and checks that they agree. The reader returns one dictionary per plot in the file; a complex AC result comes back as complex numpy arrays.

items: -o file keeps a batch run's messages; in a script, echo > file and print > file write your own.

set ngdebug prints much more about parsing and analyses; option list and option node print the expanded netlist and node table; listing (or listing expand) shows the netlist after subcircuit and parameter expansion, the most useful command when a netlist does not mean what you think.
rusage prints time and memory; option acct after each analysis.

blocks.title: Batch to PNG
blocks.text: On a server with no display, how do you produce a PNG of v(out) from a transient in a batch run?
solution: set gnuplot_terminal=png/quit then gnuplot name v(out) (gnuplot must be installed), or set pyplot_terminal=png then pyplot name v(out) (Python with matplotlib). Or wrdata the vectors and plot them with any tool.
blocks.answer: gnuplot or pyplot with the png terminal variable set, or wrdata.

items: H. Vogt, G. Atkinson, D. Warning and P. Nenzi, Ngspice User's Manual, version 47, 2026 (ngspice.sourceforge.io/docs.html), sections 11.6 (batch output), 13.5 (print, wrdata, write, plot, hardcopy, gnuplot, pyplot), 14.6 to 14.8 and 15 (rawfile format).
